notes.meaning: David walked away from his angry brother and asked other soldiers about the challenge. He wanted to confirm what was being offered and to make sure someone stood up for God's honor. His steady questioning helped spread the word until it reached the leaders.

Soldiers in the camp overheard David speaking with such bold faith that they reported it directly to King Saul. Saul was desperate for someone to answer the giant, so he summoned the young shepherd to his royal tent.

David told the king not to lose heart, offering himself to go and fight Goliath. While all the seasoned soldiers were frozen in fear, a young shepherd showed real courage because his confidence was in God rather than human strength.
Saul told David he stood no chance against the Philistine. The king pointed out that David was only a youth without battle experience, whereas Goliath had been trained in warfare since his boyhood.

David explained to Saul how he had protected his father's sheep when wild beasts attacked them. On separate occasions, when a lion or a bear snatched a lamb, David chased it down, struck it, pulled the lamb from its mouth, and killed the beast when it turned on him.
David declared that this pagan Philistine would end up just like the lion and the bear. Because Goliath dared to insult the armies of the living God, David was sure God would bring him down.

David did not boast in his own strength, but praised the Lord who had rescued him from the wild animals and promised that the Lord would rescue him from Goliath too. Hearing such deep faith, Saul gave his consent and blessed him.

Saul placed his own royal armor, a bronze helmet, and a sword onto David to protect him. David tried to walk in the heavy gear, but he took it all off because he was not trained to fight in heavy military armor.

David picked up his wooden shepherd's staff and chose five smooth stones from the stream bed, placing them in his pouch. With his familiar sling in his hand, he stepped out across the valley toward the giant.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Latin church fathers, such as Augustine, saw the five smooth stones as a symbol of the five books of Moses (the Pentateuch) chosen from the stream of the law to overcome the enemy.

notes.meaning: Goliath strode forward with a soldier carrying an enormous full-body shield ahead of him. When the giant looked down and saw only a handsome, ruddy-faced youth instead of an armed champion, he felt deeply insulted and despised him.

Goliath shouted at David, asking if he was a dog that someone would come at him with walking sticks, and he called down curses on David by the names of the Philistine gods. He taunted the boy to come close so he could feed his corpse to the wild birds and beasts.

David answered that Goliath was relying on physical weapons like the sword, spear, and javelin. David came against him in the name and authority of the Lord of Hosts, the true Commander of Israel's armies whom Goliath had insulted.

David boldly announced that the Lord would give him victory that very day by striking Goliath down and feeding the Philistine army to the scavengers. This triumph would prove to the whole earth that Israel's God is real, and it would teach God's people that the Lord does not need military weapons to save.
When Goliath began advancing across the valley toward him, David did not cower or back away. Instead, he ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the enemy head-on.

David reached into his pouch, loaded a stone into his sling, and hurled it with great speed. The stone struck the giant's exposed forehead and sank into his skull, causing him to crash face down on the earth.
David won the contest against the giant using only a shepherd's sling and a single stone. He brought down the champion of the Philistines without holding any military sword in his hand.

David ran over to the fallen giant, drew Goliath's heavy sword from its sheath, and cut off his head to prove he was completely dead. When the Philistine soldiers saw their mighty hero lifeless on the ground, panic swept through them and they ran for their lives.

The soldiers of Israel and Judah raised a great victory shout and chased the fleeing Philistines all the way to their fortified cities of Gath and Ekron, leaving dead bodies along the road. After the chase, the Israelite troops returned and took the valuable goods left behind in the enemy camp.

David brought Goliath's severed head to the area of Jerusalem, while keeping the giant's armor and weapons in his own dwelling. Displaying the head served as a visible trophy of God's victory over a terrifying enemy.

As David went out to fight, King Saul asked his army commander, Abner, who the young man's father was. Abner swore that he did not know, so the king ordered him to find out the young man's family background.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) omits these verses along with parts of the surrounding chapter, suggesting the story of Saul asking about David may come from an alternate ancient account of David's rise.

notes.meaning: When David came back from the battlefield carrying Goliath's head, Abner brought him before Saul. When the king asked who his father was, David humbly replied that he was the son of Jesse the Bethlehemite.
